Putting greens on Alafaya's larger 1990s lots

A green's price starts at the low end of $14–$30 a square foot and climbs toward the top with contouring and cups, landing most Alafaya builds around $18–$25 this year. Room for one is the real filter here, and that usually means an older, larger Waterford Lakes or Eastwood parcel rather than the newer townhome product closer to campus.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Which Alafaya lots actually have room for a green

Alafaya doesn't have a golf-course community anchoring it the way some Central Florida towns do, so the demand here is almost entirely backyard practice space rather than a lot chosen for its fairway view. The candidates are usually the wider, deeper parcels from the original Waterford Lakes and Eastwood plats, where the house sits well forward of a rear property line that often meets a pond. That distance between patio and water is exactly where a two- or three-cup green with a chipping apron fits, once the 10 ft setback from the bank is marked off.

A zero-lot-line townhome closer to UCF almost never has the run of grass a green needs, so for those addresses we're usually pointing people toward a small putting-adjacent patch of regular turf instead of a dedicated green.

Keeping light infill from sliding down a tiered green

A Alafaya green's tiers create slopes a flat lawn never has to deal with, and infill brushed in at a light, even rate can still migrate slowly toward the lowest tier over months of rinsing and rain, thinning the higher ground while building up at the bottom. That's a version of the state's rule against infill leaving a property, just moving within the green's own footprint instead of off the lot entirely. A slightly heavier grooming pass on upper tiers during routine care, rather than a different infill product altogether, is usually enough to counter the drift before it changes how a ball rolls across the surface.

A worked example: a 340 sq ft green on an Eastwood lot

Say an Eastwood backyard has 340 sq ft available for a green once the pond setback is staked off, enough for a contoured two-cup layout with a fringe collar and a small chipping pad. At $14–$30 a square foot, that project prices between $4,760 and $10,200, with the contouring and fringe work usually landing it in the $18–$25 band rather than the entry end. Most of that cost sits in shaping the base correctly, not in the putting-surface turf itself, since a flat green with a wrong break is a redo, not a repair.

Building a green over Alafaya's sandy base

The subgrade work is where a putting green earns its price over a flat lawn: contouring the compacted base to hold a break, rather than just grading it flat, has to happen in the crushed-rock layer itself, because turf laid over an uneven base just telegraphs every dip and high spot into the roll. On the area's sandy flatwoods soil, that means building the contour in compacted lifts the same way a flat lawn's base goes down, just shaped rather than sloped in one direction, with the fringe turf and cups set once the contoured base has been checked with a level in more than one direction.

Damp low tiers after a storm aren't necessarily a problem

A properly built Alafaya green's lowest tier can stay visibly damp for an hour or two after a hard summer storm even when the base underneath is draining exactly as designed, simply because water collects there briefly before working through the rock and native sand below. Mistaking that normal delay for a drainage failure and digging into a functioning base to fix it creates a real problem out of a temporary, expected one. A low tier that's still holding water the next day, well past a normal storm's drainage window, is the actual signal worth investigating, not dampness that clears within a couple of hours.

Letting the sand under a green keep draining

The state's rule against over-compacting the subgrade so tightly that it stops draining applies to a putting green exactly as it does to a lawn, even though a green's base gets shaped and hand-worked far more than a flat lawn base ever does. Native sand under a Alafaya green still needs to percolate water down and away, since a shaped base sitting on sealed-off sand just holds rainwater in its lowest tier rather than passing it through to the ground below. Contouring the rock layer for playability can't come at the cost of leaving the sand underneath unable to do its job.

Fitting a green around a pond-lot setback

On a lot where the buildable yard already loses ground to the state's waterbody setback, the green's footprint has to be planned around whatever's left rather than assumed first. That usually means a shorter green with a tighter chipping apron instead of the longer layout a full-acre lot could carry, and it's worth deciding the green's shape before ordering turf rather than after, since the setback doesn't flex for a green any more than it does for a lawn. Stimp, nap and pile direction matter more on a green than on any other service we install, since they're what makes the roll true.

Seaming the putting surface and fringe as separate pieces

The short putting surface and the taller fringe turf around a Alafaya green get cut and seamed as two distinct pieces rather than one continuous roll, since they're different products at different pile heights doing different jobs. That seam is placed deliberately along the design's edge line so it reads as a mowing transition once grooming is finished, not as a visible patch where two products meet. Getting this seam line right the first time matters more on a green than on a lawn, since the edge is exactly where a chip shot lands and a rough transition is the most visible spot on the entire surface.

Clearing debris from a green's low tiers

Leaves and pine needles collect fastest in a Alafaya green's low tiers, the same spots already doing the most drainage work, and letting debris sit there breaks it down into the infill and can slow water movement exactly where the base needs to move it fastest. Clearing those low spots promptly after they accumulate, rather than waiting for a general yard cleanup, keeps both the roll and the drainage performing as designed. A green with several tiers takes a few extra minutes to check compared with a flat lawn, since debris doesn't distribute evenly across a shaped surface.

Questions people ask

Is there room for a putting green on a typical Alafaya townhome lot?

Rarely. Townhome and zero-lot-line yards near campus are usually too narrow for a green with a real chipping apron. The larger original Waterford Lakes and Eastwood lots are the better candidates.

Does the pond setback shrink a green's usable size?

It can, since the 10 ft waterbody line and any swale beside it come off the buildable footprint the same as they would for a lawn. Sizing the green after staking the setback avoids redesigning it midway through.
